dataset.name: WattPair Appliance Load & Surge Provenance Dataset
dataset.description: Running watts, start-up surge, duty cycle and annual energy for 38 household and off-grid appliance classes, where every figure carries the source document it was read from, the tier of that source, the date it was verified and a confidence rating. The distinguishing property is not coverage but provenance: fields we have found no published figure for are present and explicitly null rather than filled with an estimate, and the basis of each surge figure is labelled (nameplate locked-rotor amperage, manufacturer-stated, category envelope, or unknown) so a reader can tell a measured inrush from a rule of thumb. Compiled from manufacturer specification sheets and manuals, government efficiency filings and standards documents. Published by WattPair under CC BY 4.0.

dataset.method: Compiled with AI assistance from manufacturer documents, government efficiency filings and standards bodies, then checked against the cited source. Every non-null figure carries the URL it was read from, so any claim here can be re-derived from public documents without trusting this file.
dataset.coverage_note: This dataset is deliberately incomplete and says where. For several appliance classes we have found no published start-up surge figure; those fields are null with a status of unknown rather than estimated, and the site makes no claim that the figure exists nowhere. Where a null field carries an absence_verified block, that block names the documents that were read and the date they were read on. Read stats.null_fields, stats.absence_verified_fields and stats.surge_basis before using any figure.
dataset.out_of_scope: Power-station records, solar-panel records, the compatibility engine and every commercial mapping are deliberately not part of this dataset.

constants.note: Two engine constant tables, without which the appliance records are not self-explanatory: a surge duration in milliseconds cannot be used correctly unless you know which band it falls in, and a missing power factor cannot be filled in without the default table. Both are derived from public standards and manufacturer documents.

appliances.name: Aquarium air pump
appliances.short_description: Household aquarium air pump. US region Aqueon QuietFlow, five tiers, 1.5–3.8 W @ 120 V 60 Hz (manufacturer tiers by tank gallons); EU region EHEIM air, three tiers, 3.5–4 W @ 50 Hz (manufacturer tiers by air output in l/h). The two regions tier along different axes, so the two ranges are not directly comparable. One of the lowest-wattage loads in this library, but because the drive mechanism cannot be verified from any source, the compatibility rating is capped at “marginal” across the board.

running_watts.test_conditions: Manufacturer Product Specifications table, row by row: 06995 Model 10 / 2-10 gallon / 1.5 W / 120V/60Hz; 06996 Model 20 / 11-20 gallon / 1.7 W; 06997 Model 40 / 40 gallon and under / 2.8 W; 06998 Model 60 / 60 gallon and under / 3.2 W; 06999 Model 100 / 100 gallon and under / 3.8 W. The manufacturer prints W directly, not amperage — there is no A×V conversion, so there is no VA-disguised-as-watts pathway here. The reasoning for taking Model 40 as the point value is in watts_distribution_note. The manufacturer does not state the test conditions (such as air outlet fully open/restricted, or back-pressure height).
running_watts.source_label: Aqueon · QuietFlow Air Pumps instruction manual, Product Specifications table (five sizes combined)

running_watts_low.test_conditions: Smallest tier on the same table: 06995 / Model 10 / Recommended Aquarium Size “2-10 gallon” / Wattage “1.5 W” / Voltage “120V/60Hz”. This is a different unit from the 2.8 W tier.

running_watts_high.test_conditions: Largest tier on the same table: 06999 / Model 100 / Recommended Aquarium Size “100 gallon and under” / Wattage “3.8 W” / Voltage “120V/60Hz”. Likewise a different unit.

absence_verified.note: Four manufacturer documents from two brands were read end to end on 2026-08-09 — Aqueon's US instruction manual covering all five QuietFlow air pump sizes, and EHEIM's three air-pump product pages. None of the four carries an inrush, start-up current, locked-rotor or peak-current figure. Aqueon's specification table lists a wattage and a mains rating per model and nothing else electrical; EHEIM's technical data lists a wattage, a frequency, an air output and a pump head, and states no voltage at all. Our search covered these four documents; we make no claim about documents we did not open.

Aqueon's manual names the pumping element without naming the drive: its maintenance section tells the owner to replace worn internal rubber diaphragms, check valves and filter pads, and its parts table lists one or two diaphragms per model. Nothing in it says what moves those diaphragms. EHEIM's product page describes noise, outlets, feet and accessories and states no drive type either. Both brands leave the electrical drive unstated, so this field is left empty and `load_type` is left at unknown rather than inferred from the word 'diaphragm'.

Neither document states a power factor, a volt-amp figure or a current. With no current published anywhere, there is not even a pair of numbers here to divide, and the field is left empty deliberately — which also keeps the engine's volt-amp gate shut on this record.

Two documents were read for a waveform requirement on 2026-08-09 and neither names one: no sentence in either mentions an inverter, a sine wave, or a waveform of any kind. Aqueon's manual does carry an extension-cord clause and a polarised-plug clause, which is the closest it comes to describing what it may be plugged into. The field is left empty rather than filled by analogy with another record.

default_duty_cycle.test_conditions: This 1.0 is a conservative value taken from a plain reading of the documents, not a duty cycle the manufacturer publishes. The manufacturer's installation steps run to five steps total, and the last step reads, verbatim, only “Plug in air pump.” — nowhere in the text is there any switch, timer, or thermostatic control, nor any record of intermittent operation; the three EHEIM pages likewise describe only noise, air outlet, feet, and accessories, with no record of any on/off control. On this basis it is treated as a continuous load. The manufacturer does not state which operating state this power consumption corresponds to.
default_duty_cycle.source_label: Aqueon · QuietFlow Air Pumps instruction manual, Installation Instructions

appliances.name: Aquarium heater
appliances.short_description: Submersible aquarium heater. The manufacturer sells it in wattage tiers by tank volume: US region Aqueon TA series 50/100/150/200/300 W @ 120 V 60 Hz; EU region EHEIM thermocontrol 25–300 W @ 50 Hz. The same wattage tier is the same number in both markets, and the tank volumes covered nearly overlap — the opposite of the electric kettle (US 1500 W / EU 3000 W). Purely resistive load; no manufacturer publishes a start-up inrush current.

This is the nameplate rated power itself, not a value converted from amperage times voltage — the manufacturer does not print amperage, so there is no VA-disguised-as-watts pathway here. The reasoning for taking TA100 as the point value is written in watts_distribution_note; it is a reviewable editorial choice, not a measurement result.

absence_verified.note: Five manufacturer documents from two brands were read end to end on 2026-08-09 — Aqueon's two US instruction manuals covering the TA and AP heater ranges, and three EHEIM thermocontrol product pages. None of the five carries an inrush, start-up current or peak-current figure. The electrical lines they do carry are a wattage per model, a mains rating on the Aqueon covers (120 Volts, 60 Hz) and a frequency on the EHEIM pages (50 Hz), all of them steady-state quantities. Our search covered these five documents; we make no claim about documents we did not open.

motor_type.test_conditions: The manufacturer's instruction manual describes no moving parts anywhere in the text: the five parts labeled in Figure 1 are the temperature dial, minimum water level line, indicator light, suction cups, and rubber guard; in the installation steps the manufacturer itself uses “heating element” to refer to the lower section of the unit (original Step 1 note: “DO NOT place suction cups over the heating element portion of the heater”). The features column of the same brand's Pro series manual separately states “No glass components” and “Electronic thermostat”. On this basis it is recorded as having no motor; `load_type=resistive` shares this same source.
motor_type.source_label: Aqueon · Submersible Aquarium Heater instruction manual (installation diagram and safety notice)

absence_verified.note: None of the three documents states a power factor or a volt-amp figure, and none states a current either, so there is not even a pair of numbers here to divide. The field is left empty deliberately, which also keeps the engine's volt-amp gate shut on this record.

Three documents were read for a waveform requirement on 2026-08-09 and none of them names one: no sentence in the three mentions an inverter, a sine wave, or a waveform of any kind. Both Aqueon manuals do carry an extension-cord clause and a polarised-plug clause, which is the closest either comes to describing what it may be plugged into. The field is left empty rather than filled by analogy with another heating record.

default_duty_cycle.test_conditions: This 1.0 is a conservative ceiling, not a duty cycle the manufacturer publishes, and not a measured average. All the manufacturer's documents support is the fact that “it switches on and off”: the Pro series manual's Power Monitor Light section states, verbatim, “Red: heating” and “Green: aquarium has reached set temperature”; the TA series manual's Step 4 likewise uses the indicator light to distinguish “functioning and in heating mode” from having reached the set temperature. The manufacturer does not publish an on/off time ratio for any tier, and this site does not derive one either — duty cycle depends on ambient room temperature, tank volume, lid, and the set-point temperature differential, all of which are user-side variables. Taking 1.0 means calculating as if the thermostat is calling for heat continuously; it yields the shortest runtime and the largest power-station threshold, which is the only acceptable rounding direction for a life-support load — for a life-support load, the direction that underestimates risk is the destructive one.
default_duty_cycle.source_label: Aqueon · Fully Submersible Aquarium Heater instruction manual (Power Monitor Light section)

appliances.name: Hair dryer
appliances.short_description: Handheld hair dryer: heating element plus blower motor. The US nameplate standard setting is 1875 W @ 110–125 V 60 Hz (the manufacturer states it ships set to 125 V; 125 V × 15 A = 1875 W, exactly the ceiling of a 15 A circuit); the EU version is officially rated 2100 W @ 220–240 V by Philips. No manufacturer publishes a wattage for each heat/speed setting, and none publishes a start-up inrush figure.

running_watts.test_conditions:
Nameplate rated power — the manufacturer prints it directly as watts. The manual’s “GETTING TO KNOW YOUR HAIR DRYER” caption reads, verbatim, “1875 watts” and “3 heat/speed settings”; the supply condition is stated verbatim in the OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS section: “Use on Alternating Current (60 hertz) only. Standard dryers are designed to operate at 110 to 125 volts AC.” Two other manuals from the same brand independently reproduce the same number: the 530 series caption likewise reads “1875 watts”, and the Model 127L features column reads “1875 watts of drying power” — three different product lines, three documents, the same number.

Basis statement (a VA-in-disguise edge case): the manual has a separate section titled “1875 WATT OPERATING GUIDE”, whose body warns that sharing a circuit with other appliances can “trip a 15 amp circuit breaker or blow a 15 amp fuse”; the Model 127L manual states “This appliance was set at the factory to operate at 125 volts”. Together these two statements show that the 1875 rating and the capacity of a 15 A circuit at 125 V are the same number. This site accepts the manufacturer-printed watts figure (see _readme item four: the manufacturer prints W directly, that amperage is a circuit-breaker rating rather than a measured current, and a hair dryer's power factor is close to 1), but it is a nameplate rating, not measured real power, and pages must not claim otherwise.
running_watts.source_label: Conair · 1875 Watt Turbo Dryer Instruction & Styling Guide (285 MODELS, US version)

absence_verified.note: Four manufacturer documents from two brands were read end to end on 2026-08-09 — Conair's instruction guides for the 285, 530 and 127L dryer lines, and Philips's product leaflet for the BHD351/10 — and none of the four carries an inrush, start-up current, peak current or locked-rotor figure. Between them the only electrical quantities they state are a wattage per model, a supply range on the Conair side (alternating current at 60 hertz, 110 to 125 volts, with a factory setting of 125 volts on the dual-voltage model) and a wattage plus a 220 to 240 volt range on the Philips side. The Conair guides do name a 15 amp circuit breaker and a 15 amp fuse, but those are the ratings of the protective devices the maker warns about tripping, not a current the dryer was measured drawing. This appliance does contain a motor, so an inrush certainly exists; what is absent is anyone publishing it. Our search covered these four documents; we make no claim about documents we did not open.

None of the three documents states a power factor or a volt-amp figure. Neither brand publishes a measured operating current either, so there is not even a pair of numbers here to divide: the only amperage anywhere in the Conair guides is the rating of a circuit breaker and a fuse. The field is left empty deliberately, which also keeps the engine's volt-amp gate shut on this record.

Three Conair guides were read for a waveform requirement on 2026-08-09 and none of them names one: no sentence in the three mentions an inverter, a sine wave, or a waveform of any kind. What they do carry about the supply is a frequency and a voltage window, a polarised-plug clause, an instruction not to run the dryer from an extension cord, and on the dual-voltage model an instruction not to use a voltage converter. That last clause is about voltage conversion, not about waveform, and is not read here as a waveform requirement. The field is left empty rather than inferred from the presence of a motor.

default_duty_cycle.test_conditions:
A hair dryer draws power continuously at the selected setting for as long as the switch is closed, with no thermostat-style on/off cycling — this is fundamentally different from a heating pad (thermostat cuts off at temperature) or a refrigerator (compressor cycling). The manufacturer's manuals describe usage throughout as continuous motion: “Move dryer steadily across each section so that the hot air passes through hair”, “Keep dryer moving as you style”, with no automatic intermittent mechanism; the only automatic cutoff the manuals mention is overheat protection (a thermal breaker) and the leakage protection on the plug, both of which are fault protection, not a working cycle. This field is therefore set to 1.0 because that is how the mechanism works, not as a conservative rounding.

1.0 means only “drawing full power at the selected setting the whole time it is on” — it does not mean the dryer runs for long stretches in a day. Actual use is a few minutes at a time, and no manufacturer publishes a duration, so typical_daily_runtime_h is left empty and daily_wh cannot be calculated.

appliances.name: Variable-speed pool pump
appliances.short_description: Variable-speed pool filter pump: the motor is driven by a variable-frequency drive, with speed settable across roughly 300–3450 RPM, so wattage varies substantially with speed. ENERGY STAR measured the same Hayward TriStar VS 950 (115 V version) under the DOE test procedure at 121 W at the low-speed measurement point and 627 W at the high-speed measurement point. The same pump wired at 230 V is certified as a separate record, with a higher rated horsepower and higher high-speed power. Single-speed pumps are outside the scope of this record.

running_watts.test_conditions:
High-speed measurement point, 115 V certification entry. The dataset row reads, verbatim: `model_name` = “TriStar VS 950”, `model_number` = “SP32950VSP (115V)”, `power_w_at_high_speed_measurement_point` = “626.95”, `rpm_at_high_speed_measurement_point` = “2177.34”, `flow_gpm_at_high_speed_measurement_point` = “60.63”, `rated_horsepower_hp` = “1.5”. The stored value of 627 is 626.95 rounded up (under-reporting the threshold by even one watt would loosen the compatibility call by that much).

This is a power reading measured on the calibration curve under the DOE pool pump test procedure — not calculated by multiplying current by voltage. The 13.2 A the manufacturer prints elsewhere is the maximum input current rating, with no conversion relationship to this value; dividing the two yields 47.5, which does not correspond to any utility voltage.

Taking the high-speed measurement point as the point value is an editorial choice; the rationale is recorded in watts_distribution_note: the low-speed point is a load almost any power station can carry, giving it no discriminating power, and the pump always runs at high speed for priming at every startup.
running_watts.source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset (Hayward TriStar VS 950, SP32950VSP 115V, pd_id 2381304)

running_watts_low.test_conditions: The low-speed measurement point for the same pump, same certification: `power_w_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “121.09”, `rpm_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “1126.02”, `flow_gpm_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “31.16”, `head_fth20_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “8.1”. The stored value of 121 is truncated (rounded down at the low end of the range, again the direction that does not loosen the determination). This is the operating condition the variable-speed pump was designed around — the Pentair manual states, verbatim: “setting the pump at the lowest speed for the longest duration is the best strategy to minimize energy consumption.”
running_watts_low.source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset (same row, low-speed measurement point)

running_watts_high.test_conditions: Same source and same measurement point as the running_watts point value (626.95 W @ 2177.34 RPM). Deliberately set equal to the point value rather than left blank: this record's point value intentionally sits at the top of the range, and the range field accurately restates that fact, which is more verifiable than a silent omission. The top of the range is not this pump's physical ceiling — 3450 RPM is, and that speed setting has no published wattage (see absence_verified under startup_surge_multiplier).
running_watts_high.source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset (same row, high-speed measurement point)

absence_verified.note: Four documents were read end to end on 2026-08-09 for an inrush, starting-current or locked-rotor figure: the EPA ENERGY STAR certified pool pump dataset, Hayward's TriStar VS 950 specification sheet, and Pentair's installation and user guides for the SuperFlo VS and the IntelliFlo VSF. None of the four carries one. The electrical quantities they do carry are all steady-state: measured power at two certified speed points, a maximum input current rating, an input voltage range, a speed range and a maximum drive input power. Two of the documents describe a variable-frequency drive that ramps the motor rather than starting it across the line, and the Pentair guide has a user-settable ramp rate, but neither states what the pump draws while ramping. A separate and larger absence is recorded alongside this one: the priming routine runs at 3450 RPM by Pentair's own default and no document in this set publishes the power drawn at that speed, so the top of this pump's real operating range is unquantified rather than merely un-surged. Our search covered these four documents; we make no claim about documents we did not open.

motor_type.test_conditions: Three documents point to the same fact, this is not an inference: (1) the ENERGY STAR dataset row has `motor_construction` = “Electronically-commutated Motor”, `motor_design` = “Variable-speed”; (2) the Hayward specification page features column reads, verbatim, “Permanent magnet, totally enclosed fan-cooled motor” and “Upgraded motor drive”; (3) the Pentair IntelliFlo VSF manual describes the drive, verbatim, as “The drive controls the motor's rotational speed by controlling the frequency of the supplied current.” Permanent magnet + electronic commutation + frequency control by a drive is exactly the definition this library uses for the `bldc_inverter` value, putting it in the same class as the mini-split-heat-pump / washing-machine / window-air-conditioner-inverter records. `load_type=inverter_driven_motor` comes from the same source as this field.
motor_type.source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset motor_construction field + Hayward specification page

absence_verified.note: Both Pentair guides list active power factor correction as a drive feature — the SuperFlo VS controller bullet list and the IntelliFlo VSF drive feature list each name it in those words — but neither states a power factor value, and the ENERGY STAR dataset carries no power factor or volt-amp column at all. A claimed capability is not a measurement. The field is left empty on purpose, which also keeps the engine's volt-amp gate shut on this record.

Both installation guides were read for a waveform requirement on 2026-08-09 and neither names one. What they do specify about the supply is a voltage window and a frequency — the SuperFlo VS guide states the pump accepts 99 to 253 Vrms at either 50 or 60 Hz single phase — plus wiring, breaker and bonding requirements. Neither mentions an inverter, a sine wave or a waveform of any kind. The field is left empty rather than filled by analogy with the other inverter-driven records in this library.

standby_watts.test_conditions: The same row's `standby_average_power_w` = “3” (Hayward TriStar VS 950, both the 115 V and 230 V certification entries report 3). The same field for the Pentair SuperFlo VST is 2. The DOE test procedure separately specifies a standby-power measurement for pool pumps, so this is a measured and reported figure, not an estimate. Note that after running the factory default schedule for 14 hours, the pump enters a stopped state rather than losing power (Pentair manual: “the pump will enter a stationary/paused state for the next 10 hours”), so this 3 W is a real daily load.
standby_watts.source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset standby_average_power_w field

default_duty_cycle.test_conditions:
While running at a given speed setting, the pump draws power continuously, with no thermostat-style on/off cycling — this is demonstrated by the manufacturer's own factory schedule: Table 2 gives SPEED 1 = 2 hours @ 3000 RPM, SPEED 2 = 10 hours @ 1400 RPM, SPEED 3 = 2 hours @ 2200 RPM, three continuous run blocks rather than a duty cycle. So taking 1.0 at the speed setting used for the determination is correct — that is how the pump actually behaves, not a conservative rounding.

Note that 1.0 describes “running continuously at a given speed setting”, not “full power for 24 hours a day”: an actual day is 14 hours running plus 10 hours stopped (see typical_daily_runtime_h), and 10 of those 14 hours are at the lowest speed setting. Multiplying 1.0 by running_watts to extrapolate full-day energy use would overstate it by more than double, which is why this library does not provide daily_wh (see energy).
default_duty_cycle.source_label: Pentair · SuperFlo VS installation and user manual (Table 2: Default Schedule)

typical_daily_runtime_h.test_conditions:
The sum of the three segments in the manufacturer's factory default schedule: SPEED 1, two hours @ 3000 RPM (starting 08:00) + SPEED 2, ten hours @ 1400 RPM + SPEED 3, two hours @ 2200 RPM = 14 hours; the manual then states, verbatim, “After 14 hours of run time and completing its run of SPEED 3, the pump will enter a stationary/paused state for the next 10 hours.”

The low confidence is deliberate: this is one manufacturer's factory default for one pump model, not an industry-typical value and not measured user behavior — actual run time depends on pool volume, water temperature, sun exposure, and local water-quality requirements, and the manufacturer itself notes on the same page that it should be adjusted for pool conditions. Any page citing it must make clear that this is a “factory default”, not “typical.”
typical_daily_runtime_h.source_label: Pentair · SuperFlo VS manual, Table 2: Default Schedule

absence_verified.note: On 2026-08-08 three Zoeller documents were opened and searched for a duty cycle, a cycles-per-hour count or a minutes-per-hour figure. Zoeller technical data sheet FM2778 (the whole MODEL COMPARISON and PRODUCT SPECIFICATIONS tables) prints HP, voltage, phase, amps, RPM, motor type, insulation class and motor protection, and no duty cycle. Installation and operating manual FM2676 prints none either; its only statement on the subject is that the installer should obtain the proper tether to customize the on-off cycle to each application — the manufacturer saying the on-off rhythm is set on site. Zoeller's own article What Is the Optimum Sump Pump Run Time? opens by stating that there is no set optimum run time for a sump pump; what it does give is installation guidance (avoid short cycling, target a minimum of one minute per cycle with at least five minutes of rest between activations, and note that fifteen to twenty cycles per hour could overheat the pump), which is an install-time setup target and not the measured duty cycle of any model. No duty cycle is derived from that guidance: the actual value is set by groundwater infiltration rate, a property of the site rather than of the machine, so this is a structural absence and not a gap a further search would close. The unblocking path is user input (pit depth, infiltration rate, on-off interval).
